paras: The attempted lynching of Francis Smith took place near Franklin Park, New Jersey, on August 5, 1905, when a posse hunting Smith, a Black farm hand, found him in a barn and nearly lynched him. Smith had been accused of trying to assault his employer's fifteen-year-old daughter the night before. A Somerville policeman brought him before a justice, who held him for the grand jury, and a Hoboken editorial later held up the case as evidence that Northerners too were roused by such accusations.

Smith worked on the farm of Jacob S. Suydam, whom the New-York Tribune called "a wealthy citizen" of the Franklin Park and Millstown area. According to a Somerville dispatch, about 10 o'clock on the night of August 4 Smith removed the screen from a bedroom window, entered the room of Suydam's daughter Adeline and tried to smother her with a pillow. The dispatch said that a second girl in the room, twelve-year-old Miss Huff, struck the intruder with the screen, cutting a deep gash in his forehead, and called for help, and that the girl's grandfather, Laurence J. Suydam, answered.

Smith escaped, and the alarm "greatly excited" the inhabitants of Franklin Park and Millstown, who formed a posse and searched the neighborhood. About 4 o'clock the next afternoon the posse found him in a barn, where, in the Tribune's words, he "narrowly escaped being lynched." The dispatch does not say how the lynching was prevented.

A later editorial in the Hoboken Observer gave a further detail: the girl's grandfather "plied the cowhide so vigorously that the culprit was glad to cry for mercy." That editorial named no one, and the Tribune's account does not mention a beating.

Robert Henderson of the Somerville police brought Smith to Somerville, where Justice Kitchen held him for the grand jury. No report of an indictment, trial or sentence was found, and no member of the posse is reported to have been charged.

The New-York Tribune carried the fullest account on August 6 under the headline "Jersey Posse Foiled. Wanted to Lynch Negro Who Attacked Girl," a heading that stated the accusation as fact. In Texas, the Waxahachie Daily Light on August 7 and the Bryan Morning Eagle on August 8 ran the same one-line item in a column of condensed news, naming the girl "Adelaide Snydam," aged fourteen, and noting that "a lynching came near resulting."

The case also drew editorial comment. The Hoboken Observer, in a piece reprinted on August 16 by the Clarke Courier of Berryville, Virginia, under the heading "Lynch Law in Jersey," opened that "it does make a difference whose ox is gored." It noted that two New Jersey mobs had been roused "almost to lynching" within two weeks, one over a farmer's murder and one over this alleged assault, and while saying "We all deplore lynch law," it called the clamor for "speedy vengeance" "most natural" when the victims were neighbors. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

The papers differ on the girl's name and age: the Somerville dispatch gave Adeline Suydam, fifteen, while the condensed Texas item gave Adelaide Snydam, fourteen. The local dispatch, which also named her father and grandfather, is the more detailed source.

A posse found Smith and he 'narrowly escaped being lynched', but he was taken alive before a justice and held for the grand jury (A1); no one was killed, so this was an attempt, not a lynching.
